**MEMORANDUM**

**To:** [Partner], M&A
**From:** [Associate]
**Re:** Pralor / Kalvesund Tankers: issues in the current transaction documents (SPA, Escrow Agreement, agreed-form TSA)
**Privileged & Confidential: Attorney Work Product**

---

## 1. Summary

I reviewed four documents:

- the Stock Purchase Agreement dated March 2, 2026 (**SPA**);
- the Escrow Agreement with Selbrook Trust Company, N.A. dated June 19, 2026 (**EA**);
- the agreed-form Transition Services Agreement (**TSA**); and
- the June 24, 2026 integration call notes.

The call notes raise no new legal issues. They are useful context on timing and on the TSA operating plan, and I have used them where relevant.

The SPA defines "Company Vessels" as **"the seven vessels owned or bareboat chartered-in by the Company listed on Schedule 1.1"** (SPA §1.1). Two of those seven are bareboat chartered-in from Torvenne Ship Leasing Ltd.: **M/T Kalvesund Aurora** and **M/T Kalvesund Borealis**. Three of the four main issues turn on how the documents treat those two vessels, or on the length of Pralor's post-Closing protection.

| # | Issue | Location | Fix type |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Torvenne change-of-control consent is not a Required Consent or a closing condition, and the indemnity carve-out leaves Pralor with no recourse | SPA Sched. 4.7 (items 2–3); §6.3 / Sched. 6.3; §8.2(c); §9.2(d) | Drafting **and client decision** |
| 2 | General reps survive only 6 months (Escrow Release Date) | SPA §9.1, §9.4; EA §1.1 ("Escrow Release Date"), §5.1 | Drafting **and client decision** |
| 3 | TSA "Company Vessels" excludes Aurora and Borealis | TSA §1.1, §2.1 (with SPA §11.9) | Drafting; small client point on fees |
| 4 | Cygnet Vessel Condition Notice was late (deadline May 6, 2026; served June 12, 2026) | SPA §6.4(a)–(c); EA Recital C, §2.1(b), §6 | **Client decision** on strategy |
| 5 | Other points: outside date, ISM handover, liability cap | SPA §10.1(b); TSA §9.5(b); SPA §9.5 | Check / drafting |

---

## 2. Issues

### Issue 1: Torvenne bareboat charter consent is not required for Closing, and Pralor has no indemnity if Torvenne terminates

**Location**

- **SPA Schedule 4.7, items 2 and 3.** Clause 31 of each BARECON 2017 charter "requires the prior written consent of the Owner to any change of control of the Charterer." If the change of control occurs without consent, Torvenne "may terminate the charter and repossess the vessel."
- **SPA §6.3 and Schedule 6.3.** Seller's consent covenant covers only the Required Consents. Schedule 6.3 lists only the Aldmoor Bank consent or payoff.
- **SPA §8.2(c).** The closing condition is limited to "each Required Consent listed on Schedule 6.3."
- **SPA §9.2(d).** Seller has no liability under §9.2(a) for "any matter disclosed in the Disclosure Schedule."
- **SPA §4.4(c).** The no-conflicts rep is qualified by Schedule 4.4, which is not in the folder. Please obtain it. It will very likely carve out the Torvenne consent as well.

**Why it matters**

The sale of the Shares is a change of control of the Charterer, so Closing will trigger Clause 31. As drafted:

- Seller only has to use efforts to obtain consents listed on Schedule 6.3, and Torvenne's consent is not on that list.
- Pralor's obligation to close does not depend on Torvenne consenting.
- Because Seller disclosed the consent requirement in Schedule 4.7, §9.2(d) removes any indemnity claim if Torvenne terminates.

Pralor could therefore pay the full $186,000,000 and then lose two of the seven tankers by repossession. That would also mean losing the charter purchase options and any employment on those vessels, with no claim against Seller.

The integration call notes cover Aldmoor (item 3.4) but say nothing about Torvenne. As far as the record shows, no one is working this consent.

**Recommended fix**

1. Add Torvenne to Schedule 6.3. The consent should be an express written consent and no-default confirmation, not just a waiver. This automatically brings the consent within both §6.3 and §8.2(c).

   > **Schedule 6.3, new item 2:** "Written consent of Torvenne Ship Leasing Ltd., as Owner under each Bareboat Charter, to the sale of the Shares to Buyer and the resulting change of control of the Company under Clause 31 (Change of Control) of the additional clauses to each Bareboat Charter, together with written confirmation that no termination event, event of default or right of repossession arises from the transactions contemplated by this Agreement, in each case without amendment to the economic terms of either Bareboat Charter (including the purchase option) and otherwise in form and substance reasonably satisfactory to Buyer."

2. Override the disclosure carve-out with a specific indemnity. This is a backstop in case Pralor waives the condition or Torvenne's consent later proves defective.

   > **New §9.2(e):** "any termination of, or exercise of any right of repossession or other remedy under, either Bareboat Charter arising out of the change of control of the Company resulting from the transactions contemplated by this Agreement, or any failure to obtain the consent of Torvenne thereto,"
   >
   > **Amend §9.2(d):** "…provided, however, that (d) Seller shall have no liability under Section 9.2(a) for any Losses arising from any matter disclosed in the Disclosure Schedule, *it being agreed that this clause (d) shall not limit Section 9.2(e).*"
   >
   > **Amend §9.5** so that the basket and the Indemnity Escrow cap do not apply to §9.2(e). That cap is $9,300,000, which is far below the value of two MR tankers.

3. Consider a fallback price mechanism for the case where Pralor elects to close without the consent. For example, a per-vessel price reduction or a dedicated escrow for each of Aurora and Borealis, released when Torvenne consents or the consent window lapses.

**Client decision needed:** Pralor should decide whether it would ever close without Torvenne's consent, and if so on what terms (specific indemnity, price reduction or separate escrow). This drives how hard we push the condition. We also need Torvenne's commercial position. If Pralor's credit profile is weaker than Seller's, Torvenne may ask for a guarantee or other credit support as the price of consenting.

---

### Issue 2: General representations survive only six months

**Location**

- **SPA §9.1.** All non-Fundamental representations survive "until the Escrow Release Date (as defined in the Escrow Agreement)."
- **SPA §9.4.** A claim is barred unless notice is delivered before the survival period expires.
- **EA §1.1.** The Escrow Release Date is "the date that is six (6) months after the Closing Date."
- **EA §§4.1 and 5.1.** Claim Notices must be delivered before that date, after which the balance is released to Seller.
- **SPA §11.9.** The EA controls on escrow mechanics. The SPA expressly adopts the EA definition, so there is no conflict for the SPA to win.

**Why it matters**

The survival period covers the reps most likely to produce post-Closing claims:

- vessel condition and class (§4.8(c)–(d));
- port state detentions and casualties (§4.8(e));
- MARPOL, ballast water and OPA 90 compliance and certificates (§4.9);
- Material Contracts (§4.7); and
- MLC compliance (§4.13).

Defects in hull, ballast-water or pollution-prevention systems, and historic flag or port state violations, typically come to light at the next annual or intermediate class survey or drydocking, or at a port state control inspection. Those events often fall more than six months after Closing.

The six-month window also coincides with the TSA term (TSA §9.1). Seller will be the technical manager for most of the survival period and will control the vessel records. Pralor's own superintendents will only see the ships independently after the claims window has largely closed. Once the window closes, the full $9,300,000 Indemnity Escrow is released to Seller (EA §5.1). Under SPA §9.5(b) and §9.6 the escrow is also the cap and the first source of recovery, so in practice Pralor would have no remedy at all.

**Recommended fix**

1. Delink survival from the escrow definition and set a stand-alone period. Pair it with a longer period for the operational and environmental reps.

   > **SPA §9.1 (replace second sentence):** "The representations and warranties in Sections 4.8 (Company Vessels) and 4.9 (Environmental and Regulatory Matters) survive the Closing until the date that is twenty-four (24) months after the Closing Date. All other representations and warranties of the parties survive the Closing until the date that is eighteen (18) months after the Closing Date."

2. Conform the EA. This requires a tri-party amendment under EA §11.2 because the EA is already signed.

   > **EA §1.1:** "'**Escrow Release Date**' means the date that is eighteen (18) months after the Closing Date…"

   Possible variant: release 50% at 12 months and the balance at 24 months, less the Pending Claim Amount.

3. Consider adding a time-bar exception for claims arising from defects identified at the first post-Closing class survey or drydocking, if that survey falls outside the period.

**Client decision needed:** Pralor should decide what survival period and escrow tail to request, and what it would trade for them. Seller will resist tying up $9.3m for longer. Pralor's technical team should tell us when each vessel's next intermediate or special survey and drydock fall due, so that we can anchor the request to the real survey cycle. This point also interacts with Issue 4 (see the alternative route described there).

---

### Issue 3: The TSA excludes the two bareboat-chartered tankers from transition services

**Location**

- **TSA §1.1.** "Company Vessels" means "the vessels **owned by the Company and registered in its name**."
- **TSA §2.1.** Technical management, crew management and ISM/ISPS services are provided "for the Company Vessels". The same term runs through Schedule A, the DOC definition, the per-vessel fees in Schedule B, and §§3.3, 3.4 and 9.5.
- **SPA §1.1.** "Company Vessels" means all seven owned *or bareboat chartered-in* vessels on Schedule 1.1.
- **SPA §11.9.** "The Transition Services Agreement controls as to Transition Services", so the broader SPA definition does not override the TSA.
- The TSA's "capitalized terms… have the meanings given in the Purchase Agreement" fallback does not help, because the TSA defines the term itself.

**Why it matters**

Aurora and Borealis are registered in Torvenne's name, not the Company's. As drafted, Seller has no obligation after Closing to manage, crew or provide ISM/DOC coverage for them. Seller's existing intra-group arrangement ends at Closing (TSA Recital B; SPA Sched. 4.7 item 4).

Without a DOC holder and valid SMCs, those two vessels cannot lawfully trade from the Closing Date. That would also put the Company in breach of the bareboat charters, which require the charterer to manage and maintain the vessels. The TSA is to be signed at Closing (SPA §§3.2(a)(iii) and 6.5), so this needs to be fixed now. The integration team's plan (call notes §4) assumes "all vessels" transition under the TSA.

**Recommended fix**

Conform the TSA definition to the SPA before the form is finalized:

> **TSA §1.1:** "'**Company Vessels**' means the seven vessels owned or bareboat chartered-in by the Company and listed on Schedule 1.1 to the Purchase Agreement, being M/T Kalvesund Aurora, M/T Kalvesund Borealis, M/T Kalvesund Cygnet, M/T Kalvesund Dawn, M/T Kalvesund Eider, M/T Kalvesund Fulmar and M/T Kalvesund Gannet, and '**Company Vessel**' means any of them."

Two follow-on changes:

- add to TSA §3.2 a covenant that Provider will perform the Transition Services for the bareboat-chartered vessels in compliance with the charterer's maintenance and management obligations under the Bareboat Charters; and
- confirm that the DOC under TSA §1.1 covers all seven vessels.

**Client point:** Because Schedule B fees are charged per vessel, this adds roughly $48,000 a month (2 × $24,000) to the TSA cost. That cost is unavoidable if the vessels are to keep trading, but Pralor's finance team should be told.

---

### Issue 4: Cygnet Vessel Condition Notice was delivered after the SPA deadline

**Location**

- **SPA Preamble.** The SPA Signing Date is March 2, 2026.
- **SPA §6.4(a).** The Inspection Period is 45 days after the SPA Signing Date, ending **April 16, 2026**.
- **SPA §6.4(b).** A Vessel Condition Notice must be delivered "within 20 days after the last day of the Inspection Period", which gives a deadline of **May 6, 2026**.
- **SPA §6.4(c).** If no timely notice is given, Buyer is "deemed to have accepted the condition" of the vessel and to have waived repair and price-reduction claims "under this Section 6.4."
- **EA Recital C, §2.1(b) and §6.** The Cygnet Notice was delivered on **June 12, 2026**, about five weeks late. Seller asserts it is untimely and Buyer disputes that. The **$2,400,000** Disputed Repair Amount is to be held in the Disputed Repair Account until a Joint Written Instruction or Final Order. Under EA §6.4, the Escrow Agent will not decide timeliness.

**Why it matters**

On the face of §6.4, Seller has a strong position. If the dispute goes to the Court of Chancery, a Delaware court is likely to enforce the deadline and deemed-acceptance language as written between sophisticated parties. The $2.4m would then go to Seller as Purchase Price (EA §6.3), and Pralor would bear the hull and cargo-system repair cost itself. The escrow holdback preserves the dispute; it does not improve Pralor's position on the merits.

Pralor has some arguments and some leverage:

1. **Access and prevention.** If Seller did not give "reasonable access to each Company Vessel at a port of call during the Inspection Period" (SPA §6.4(a)), Pralor may argue Seller prevented timely inspection. We need the facts from the client.
2. **The waiver is limited to §6.4.** Section 6.4(c) waives claims "under this Section 6.4" only. A claim for breach of §4.8(c)–(d) (seaworthiness, good condition, maintenance) under §9.2(a) arguably survives. Such a claim would be subject to:
   - the $930,000 basket;
   - the escrow cap;
   - the §9.2(d) disclosure carve-out, so we must check whether the defects are disclosed; and
   - the six-month survival window in Issue 2.
3. **Closing condition.** The reps are brought down at Closing (Article IV lead-in; §8.2(a)). If the Cygnet defects make §4.8(d) materially untrue, the bring-down condition gives Pralor negotiating leverage before Closing.

**Recommended fix**

Try to resolve this commercially before Closing rather than litigate after it. In order of preference:

- **(a) Written waiver by Seller** of the §6.4(b) deadline for the Cygnet Notice, signed as required by SPA §11.3. For example:

  > "Seller irrevocably waives any objection that the Vessel Condition Notice dated June 12, 2026 in respect of M/T Kalvesund Cygnet was not delivered within the period required by Section 6.4(b), and agrees that such notice shall be treated for all purposes of this Agreement and the Escrow Agreement as a timely Vessel Condition Notice. Section 6.4(c) shall not apply to M/T Kalvesund Cygnet in respect of the defects identified in that notice."

- **(b) Agreed price reduction** in a negotiated amount, documented by SPA amendment, with a Joint Written Instruction releasing the Disputed Repair Account accordingly.
- **(c) Specific indemnity** for the identified Cygnet hull and cargo-system defects, outside the basket, the cap and the §9.2(d) carve-out.

**Client decision needed:** Pralor should choose between pressing for a full waiver, accepting a negotiated split, or pursuing the dispute after Closing. Pralor should understand that its litigation position on timeliness is weak. We should also ask the client for the inspection timeline and access history, which bear on argument 1 above.

---

### Issue 5: Other points to check

1. **Outside date (SPA §10.1(b)).** Either party may terminate if Closing has not occurred by **September 30, 2026**. The call notes targeted a late-July Closing. If Closing has not yet occurred and the date has not been extended in writing, Seller currently has a walk right, which affects our leverage on every point above. Please confirm the status. If Closing has not occurred, we should either seek a written extension or confirm that Pralor accepts the risk (**client decision**).
2. **ISM handover (TSA §9.5(b)).** Provider maintains DOC and SMS coverage after termination "for no longer than 30 days." If interim DOC or SMC issuance to the replacement manager slips, the vessels could be left uncovered. I suggest changing the limit to "until an interim DOC and interim SMC have been issued… and in any event for not less than 60 days." This matters most given the six-month term and Pralor's target of migrating within the initial term (call notes §4.1).
3. **Liability cap (SPA §9.5(b)).** General rep liability is capped at the $9,300,000 Indemnity Escrow Amount, about 5% of the price. This is a commercial point that Pralor may already have accepted. It becomes more important if Issues 1 and 4 are pushed into the indemnity rather than resolved before Closing.
4. **Schedule 4.4.** This schedule is referenced but missing from the folder. We should obtain it to confirm what conflicts and consents it carves out of §4.4(c).

---

## 3. Points for the client call

1. **Torvenne.** Will Pralor close without Torvenne's consent? If yes, on what protection? Who will approach Torvenne, and should Pralor offer credit support?
2. **Survival and escrow.** What survival period and escrow tail should we request (we suggest 18/24 months)? We also need the vessels' survey and drydock schedule.
3. **Cygnet.** Should we seek a waiver, a price reduction or a specific indemnity? Or reserve the point for post-Closing litigation, knowing the timeliness argument is weak? We also need the inspection access history.
4. **TSA fees.** Note the additional cost (about $48k a month) of covering Aurora and Borealis.
5. **Timing.** What is the status of the September 30, 2026 outside date?

The TSA definition fix (Issue 3) and the ISM handover change can go into our markup now. Issues 1, 2 and 4 need instructions before we take a final position with Seller.

# MEMORANDUM

**To:** [Partner], M&A
**From:** [Associate]
**Re:** Pralor Maritime Holdings, LLC / Acquisition of Kalvesund Tankers, Inc.: Buyer-side issues in current transaction documents
**Privileged & Confidential: Attorney Work Product**

---

## Executive Summary

I reviewed four documents:

- the Stock Purchase Agreement dated March 2, 2026 (**SPA**);
- the Escrow Agreement with Selbrook Trust Company, N.A. dated June 19, 2026 (**EA**);
- the agreed-form Transition Services Agreement (**TSA**); and
- the June 24, 2026 integration call notes.

The call notes are operational. They do not raise new drafting points, but they confirm Pralor's expectation that **all** vessels will be managed under the TSA until migration (notes §4.1).

The three most significant exposures, in order, are:

1. **Torvenne change-of-control consent is not a Seller obligation or a closing condition.** Pralor could close and then lose two of the seven tankers to repossession, with no indemnity recourse.
2. **The TSA excludes the two bareboat-chartered tankers.** The TSA's narrower definition of "Company Vessels" leaves M/T Kalvesund Aurora and M/T Kalvesund Borealis without technical management, crewing or ISM/DOC cover from Closing. Under SPA §11.9, the TSA controls on services.
3. **General representations survive only six months.** Survival is pegged to an Escrow Release Date of six months after Closing. That is too short for vessel-condition and MARPOL/environmental claims, and the $9.3m escrow is released before such defects typically surface.

The secondary points are listed in Part B. The items needing **client decisions** are flagged with ⚑ and collected in Part C.

---

## A. Principal Issues

### 1. Torvenne bareboat charter change-of-control consent omitted from Required Consents and closing conditions ⚑

**Location**
- SPA Schedule 4.7, items 2 and 3 (Clause 31 of each Torvenne BARECON 2017 charter)
- SPA §6.3 and Schedule 6.3 (Required Consents)
- SPA §8.2(c) (closing condition)
- SPA §9.2(d) (disclosed-matter carve-out)

**What the documents say**
- **Schedule 4.7.** Each Torvenne charter "requires the prior written consent of the Owner to any change of control of the Charterer." If consent is not given, Torvenne "may terminate the charter and repossess the vessel."
- **Schedule 6.3.** Lists only the Aldmoor Bank consent or payoff.
- **Seller's covenant (§6.3).** Seller need only use commercially reasonable efforts to obtain the Schedule 6.3 consents.
- **Closing condition (§8.2(c)).** Requires only the Schedule 6.3 consents.
- **Indemnity carve-out (§9.2(d)).** Seller has no §9.2(a) liability for matters disclosed in the Disclosure Schedule.

**Why it matters**
- The sale of the Shares is itself the change of control that triggers Clause 31.
- As drafted, Seller has no obligation to seek Torvenne's consent, and Pralor has no condition entitling it to refuse to close.
- Because the consent requirement is disclosed in Schedule 4.7, §9.2(d) bars an indemnity claim. Any argument under the §4.4(c) no-conflicts representation fails for the same reason.
- If Torvenne terminates after Closing, Pralor loses two of seven tankers, roughly 29% of the fleet. Those are MR tonnage on seven-year charters with purchase options. Pralor would also lose any value attributed to those options, and its only recourse would be to renegotiate with Torvenne.

**Recommended fix**

Add the Torvenne consents to Schedule 6.3, as new item 2:

> "2. Written consent of Torvenne Ship Leasing Ltd., as Owner under each Bareboat Charter, pursuant to Clause 31 of the additional clauses thereto, to the sale of the Shares to Buyer and the resulting change of control of the Company, together with written confirmation that (a) no termination right, event of default or right to repossess arises under either Bareboat Charter as a result of the transactions contemplated by this Agreement, and (b) the purchase option under each Bareboat Charter remains in full force and effect, in each case in form and substance reasonably satisfactory to Buyer."

This flows automatically into §6.3 and §8.2(c).

Add a specific indemnity as a fallback, in case Pralor elects to close without the consent. New §9.2(e):

> "(e) any termination of, or exercise of any right of repossession or other remedy under, either Bareboat Charter arising out of the change of control of the Company effected by this Agreement, notwithstanding Section 9.2(d), any disclosure in the Disclosure Schedule, Section 9.5 or Section 9.6."

Add a conforming carve-out to the §9.2(d) proviso: "other than with respect to the matters described in Section 9.2(e)."

**⚑ Client decision.** Pralor should decide whether the Torvenne consent is a **walk-right** (hard closing condition) or whether it would close on a specific indemnity, escrow or price holdback.
- If it would close on a holdback, Pralor must agree a value per vessel. Finance should be asked what value is attributed to each Torvenne charter and its purchase option.
- Pralor should also consider whether Seller's obligation should be raised from "commercially reasonable efforts" to an absolute obligation to deliver the Torvenne consents.

---

### 2. TSA definition of "Company Vessels" excludes M/T Kalvesund Aurora and M/T Kalvesund Borealis

**Location**
- TSA §1.1 ("Company Vessels")
- TSA §2.1 and Schedule A (scope of services)
- TSA §5.1 and Schedule B (fees)
- TSA §9.5(b) (post-termination DOC cover)
- SPA §1.1 ("Company Vessels") and SPA §11.9 (order of precedence)

**What the documents say**
- **SPA §1.1.** Defines "Company Vessels" as "the seven vessels owned or bareboat chartered-in by the Company listed on Schedule 1.1."
- **TSA §1.1.** Defines "Company Vessels" as "the vessels owned by the Company and registered in its name."
  - The two Torvenne tankers are registered in Torvenne's name. Schedule 1.1 shows them as "Bareboat chartered-in from Torvenne."
  - The TSA definition therefore captures only the five owned vessels: Cygnet, Dawn, Eider, Fulmar and Gannet.
- **TSA §2.1.** Seller's technical management, crew management and ISM/ISPS obligations, including acting as ISM "Company," maintaining the DOC and SMCs, and providing the DPA, apply only "for the Company Vessels."
- **SPA §11.9.** The TSA "controls as to Transition Services." The SPA's broader definition therefore does not cure the gap. The TSA's own definitional clause also overrides the general incorporation of SPA definitions in TSA §1.1.

**Why it matters**
- At Closing, the intra-group management arrangement terminates (TSA Recital B; SPA Schedule 4.7, item 4).
- Aurora and Borealis would have no contracted technical manager, no crew manager, and no ISM "Company" holding a DOC that covers them.
- A vessel without a valid DOC/SMC cannot lawfully trade. It is exposed to flag-state and port state control action, and potentially to breach of the Torvenne charters, which will require proper management and class maintenance.
- This is inconsistent with what Pralor expects. The call notes (§4.1) assume all vessels move under the TSA and then migrate within six months.
- Pralor would have no contractual right to compel Seller to manage these vessels. Under TSA §2.3, Seller need only "consider the request in good faith," at a fee agreed at the time.

**Recommended fix**

Conform the TSA definition to the SPA before the agreed form is signed at Closing. TSA §1.1:

> "'**Company Vessels**' means the seven vessels owned or bareboat chartered-in by the Company listed on Schedule 1.1 to the Purchase Agreement (including M/T Kalvesund Aurora and M/T Kalvesund Borealis), and '**Company Vessel**' means any of them."

Make the following conforming points:
- Confirm that the DOC definition and Schedule A, Part 3 (DOC/SMS/SMC) expressly cover the bareboat-chartered vessels.
- Confirm that Schedule B fees apply to all seven vessels. Total cost is $24,000 × 7 = $168,000 per month, and finance should budget on that basis.
- Consider adding an obligation on Provider to comply with the technical, class and insurance requirements of the Bareboat Charters. Add "and the Bareboat Charters" to TSA §3.2.

This is a drafting change. Because the TSA is an "agreed form," we should raise it with Seller as a conforming correction rather than a renegotiation.

---

### 3. General representations survive only six months (via the EA's Escrow Release Date) ⚑

**Location**
- SPA §9.1 (survival)
- SPA §9.4 (time bar)
- SPA §9.5(b) and §9.6 (cap and source of recovery)
- EA §1.1 ("Escrow Release Date")
- EA §§4.1 and 5.1 (claim notices and release)

**What the documents say**
- **SPA §9.1.** All non-Fundamental Representations survive "until the Escrow Release Date (as defined in the Escrow Agreement)." This includes §4.7 (Material Contracts), §4.8 (Company Vessels: class, seaworthiness, detentions) and §4.9 (Environmental/ISM/MARPOL/BWM).
- **EA §1.1.** Defines the Escrow Release Date as "the date that is six (6) months after the Closing Date."
- **SPA §9.4.** Bars any representation-based claim not noticed before that date.
- **EA §5.1.** Releases the $9,300,000 Indemnity Escrow Amount to Seller on that date, net of pending claims.
- **SPA §9.5(b).** The escrow amount is also Seller's cap for §9.2(a) claims.
- **SPA §11.9.** Gives the EA control over escrow mechanics. The SPA simply adopts the EA definition, so there is no conflict to resolve in Pralor's favor.

**Why it matters**
- Six months is materially shorter than market for vessel and environmental representations, where 18 to 24 months is common.
- Hull, ballast-water, pollution-prevention and cargo-system defects usually surface at the next annual or intermediate class survey or drydocking, during SIRE/vetting, or at port state control inspection.
  - Many of those events will fall outside a six-month window.
  - TSA Schedule A, Part 1, item 4 contemplates drydockings "scheduled during the Term" only, which is also six months.
- MARPOL and OPA 90 exposure from historical non-compliance can take longer still to come to light.
- Under the current drafting, Pralor's recovery for an operational or environmental breach would likely be time-barred, and the escrow would already have been released.
- The six-month TSA term compounds the problem. Pralor will still be running on Seller's management and records for most of the survival period, so it is poorly placed to identify breaches quickly.

**Recommended fix**

The EA is signed (June 19, 2026), so this requires an **amendment to both the SPA and the EA**, signed by Buyer, Seller and Selbrook (EA §11.2).

SPA §9.1, replace the second sentence:

> "The representations and warranties in Sections 4.7, 4.8, 4.9 and 4.13 survive the Closing until the date that is twenty-four (24) months after the Closing Date. All other representations and warranties of the parties survive the Closing until the date that is eighteen (18) months after the Closing Date."

EA §1.1, revise the definition:

> "'**Escrow Release Date**' means the date that is [eighteen (18)][twenty-four (24)] months after the Closing Date. If that date is not a Business Day, the Escrow Release Date is the next Business Day."

Alternatively, provide a staged release, for example 50% at 12 months and the balance at 24 months, net of pending claims.

Decouple survival from the escrow definition. Define the survival periods in the SPA itself, so that a future change to the EA cannot shorten Pralor's claim window.

**⚑ Client decision.** Pralor should decide its commercial target:
- the survival length it wants;
- whether to accept a staged release; and
- whether to trade on the $930,000 basket or the escrow-based cap (§9.5).

Pralor's Technical/HSQE team should confirm when the next class surveys and drydockings fall for each vessel. That timeline should drive the ask.

## B. Secondary Points

### 4. Seller's consent covenant is efforts-based only
**Location:** SPA §6.3.

**Issue:** Seller need only use "commercially reasonable efforts." Combined with item 1, this is weak for consents that are existential to the deal value.

**Fix:** Making the Torvenne consent a closing condition largely solves the problem. Additionally, consider requiring Seller to provide copies of all correspondence with Torvenne, and to give Buyer the right to participate in discussions.

### 5. Indemnity cap equals the escrow amount (5% of price)
**Location:** SPA §9.5(b) and §9.6.

**Issue:** The cap on general representations is $9.3m, about 5% of the $186m Purchase Price. A single serious casualty, MARPOL prosecution or loss of a charter could exceed it.

**Fix ⚑:** This is a commercial point for Pralor. Options include:
- carving §4.8 and §4.9 out of the general cap, or setting a higher sub-cap (for example 15–20%); or
- treating them as quasi-fundamental.

At a minimum, any specific Torvenne indemnity (item 1) must sit outside the cap.

### 6. TSA term and DOC tail are tight
**Location:** TSA §9.1 and §9.5(b).

**Issue:** The initial term is six months, with one three-month extension on 30 days' notice. Post-termination DOC/SMS cover is "no longer than 30 days." If interim DOC/SMC issuance to the replacement manager slips, vessels could fall out of ISM cover.

**Fix:** Revise TSA §9.5(b) to read "until an interim DOC and interim SMC have been issued to the replacement manager, *and in any event for not less than 30 days*, and thereafter for up to a further 60 days on the Company's request." Also diarize the extension notice deadline (initial term end minus 30 days).

### 7. Provider liability cap
**Location:** TSA §7.1.

**Issue:** Liability is capped at ten times the annual fees per affected vessel, about $2.88m per vessel. That is standard BIMCO/SHIPMAN-style, but Pralor should be comfortable with it given that Seller also stands behind the vessel representations.

**Fix:** No change is required unless Pralor wishes to push. Ensure that TSA claims and SPA indemnity claims are not treated as overlapping or duplicative.
